name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
label: Gyeongbokgung
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5501517: large area 'Gyeongbokgung Palace' (1030 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The largest and most famous royal palace of the Joseon dynasty.

text.description: Gyeongbokgung was the first royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, established in 1395, and it is now one of the most significant tourist attractions in South Korea. It photographs well because the grounds are large and open, with long stretches of tiled roofs, stone paving and timber halls that give your pictures plenty of depth and pattern. The palace flourished under Sejong the Great, and Hangul, the Korean script, was developed here during his reign. It has a turbulent story too. It was burned down in 1592 during the Imjin War and left unused for around 270 years, then rebuilt in the 1860s. During the colonial period most of its roughly 500 buildings were sold off or demolished, and by 1945 only 40 pre-colonial buildings remained. Restoration since the 1980s has recreated dozens of them. For photos, plan on a mix of wide views and close details. Start with a wide shot to show the scale of the courtyards, then move in on painted eaves, doorways and stonework. A changing of the guard ceremony takes place twice a day, which adds colour and movement if you time your visit for it. Please be considerate when people wander into your frame. Check the official site for current visiting arrangements before you go.
text.geographic_location: Gyeongbokgung Palace is in Seoul, South Korea, and covers a large area.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so start from central Seoul and take a taxi to Gyeongbokgung Palace. The palace also has its own subway stop, Gyeongbokgung Station. Once you are at the palace, follow the map to the phone icon on the map, then look north towards the palace. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a courtyard and the buildings around it in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, painted beams and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the main hall or gate on a vertical line, keeping the horizon level so the long rooflines do not slope. Include a bit of paving in the foreground to add depth. Take one wide shot and then zoom in for a few detail shots. Wait a moment for people to pass if you want a clearer view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the roof colours do not wash out. Try a Live Photo for the guard ceremony or for moving crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The palace is open at night for part of the year, so check the official site for dates before planning an evening visit.

text.access_note: Check the official site for current visiting and entry details before you go.

name: Sungnyemun (Namdaemun)
label: Namdaemun Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '서울로7017' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '서울로 7017' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10647050: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sungnyemun Gate;Sungnyemun (Gate)' (55 m across).
notes: Historic city gate, Korea's National Treasure No. 1.

text.description:
Sungnyemun, also called Namdaemun or the South Great Gate, is the southern gate of the old Seoul City Wall. It stands in Jung District, with the busy Namdaemun Market right beside it. The gate was first built in 1398 and rebuilt in 1447. It was named South Korea's National Treasure No. 1 in 1962. In February 2008 a fire destroyed the wooden upper storey, and after a long restoration the gate reopened in May 2013. It photographs well because the two-tiered tiled roof sits in the middle of a modern city of traffic, towers and market streets. That contrast is the picture.

From up there you look down over the station and the streets towards Namdaemun Market, and the gate appears as part of the wider scene rather than filling the frame. This makes a calmer alternative to standing at street level. For a close, full view of the gate, walk over and shoot from outside it. It is framed by the surrounding city and lit up in the evening. Keep the gate itself in the frame rather than cropping the roof, and use the city lights around it to add depth.
text.geographic_location: Sungnyemun is in Jung District in central Seoul, between Seoul Station and Seoul Plaza, with Namdaemun Market next to it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. 서울로7017 is the elevated walkway over Seoul Station, and you can reach it by lift, stairs or ramp. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of station, streets and gate. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the gate closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the walkway and the city in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 서울로7017 (elevated walkway over Seoul Station, reached by lift, stairs or ramp). A looking-down view over Seoul Station and the streets toward Namdaemun Market, with the gate in the wider scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gate on one of the lines, with the streets leading towards it. If the gate looks small, zoom in rather than walking away from the railing. For a full, close view of the two-storey wooden roof, shoot from outside the gate itself instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lit roof and city lights do not wash out. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or night, when the city-view lighting is on and the gate is lit up.

text.access_note: 서울로7017 is a public elevated walkway, but the gate's grounds may close to visitors at certain times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Namdaemun Market
label: Namdaemun Market
camera_source: Commons cluster (10 photos). Moved 118 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/78503350: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Namdaemun Market' (454 m across).
notes: The oldest and largest traditional market in Seoul.

text.description: Namdaemun Market is a big, busy traditional market right beside Namdaemun, the main southern gate of the old city. It opened in 1414, in the Joseon period, which makes it one of the oldest markets in Korea that still operates. Fires have destroyed it several times, including one during the Korean War, and each time it was rebuilt to roughly the same size. Today it is modernised but still lively. A 2016 count by the Seoul Institute listed about 5,200 stores and 9,090 workers across roughly 64,600 square metres. That scale is what makes it good for photos. You get crowded lanes, stacked goods, hanging signs and people at work, all in strong colour and close to hand. A phone suits this kind of picture well. Take one wide shot to show the busy lane, then move in on the details: a pile of goods, a handwritten sign, a vendor's hands. Keep your elbows in, step to the side of the walkway before you stop, and ask before you photograph anyone up close, since these are people's workplaces. Check the exposure after each shot, because bright signs and dark awnings can fool the camera.
text.geographic_location: In central Seoul, next to Namdaemun, the main southern gate of the old city.
text.directions_text: Head for Namdaemun, the old city's main southern gate, which the market sits beside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for lane scenes. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in tight, crowded aisles, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for stall details without leaning into people's space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kalguksu Alley (narrow lane of noodle stalls inside Namdaemun Market). Vendors' bowls of handmade noodle soup in a narrow lane, with rising steam and colorful ingredients in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a lane up with the centre so it leads the eye into the picture. Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then a closer one of a single stall or product. Keep the phone straight to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone area to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright signs and lights don't wash out. Try portrait mode on goods piled on a stall, and use Live Photos for moving crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day usually means fewer people and easier framing, and the market has long been known for its morning trade. Daylight also keeps colours true, so use night mode only if you shoot after dark.

text.access_note: This is a working market with many separate shops and stalls, so check the official site before you go for opening days and times.
claims_not_in_sources: Namdaemun Market is in Seoul's Jung District.
The lanes of the market are often narrow and crowded.
Earlier in the day the market is typically less crowded than around midday.
Many stalls have bright signs and awnings that can make exposure tricky.
Stallholders may prefer to be asked before being photographed close up.

name: Gwanghwamun Square
label: Gwanghwamun Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '세종대왕 동상' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '광화문광장 세종대왕동상' (way/380883710): middle (8 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5672803: 'Cheugugi(Rain Gauge)', the best-known feature inside 'Gwanghwamun Square' (529 m across).
notes: Wide boulevard plaza with the statues of King Sejong and Admiral Yi.

text.description:
Gwanghwamun Square is a broad public square on Sejongno, laid out in front of Gyeongbokgung palace. For centuries this ground was the Street of Six Ministries, home to the royal administrative buildings. Today it is a long, open pedestrian space with fountains, a shallow waterway and two statues. It photographs well because the sightlines are so clear: from the right spot you can line up a statue, the palace gate and the trees beyond in a single frame.

The best-known photo here is King Sejong the Great. The bronze statue is 6.2 metres high and weighs 20 tons. It was unveiled on 9 October 2009, a couple of months after the square first opened. It sits about 250 metres on from the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, so you can see how much room the square gives you. The square was closed for redesign from the end of 2020, and the larger pedestrian plaza reopened on 6 August 2022. That means older photos online may not match what you see.

Stand by the King Sejong statue and look north: Gwanghwamun Gate and the trees at the far end sit behind the seated king. Guides suggest the statue looks even better once it is lit after dark. If you have time, the pine trees at 육조마당 make a good alternative with the gate and Bugaksan Mountain behind. Events and festivals sometimes fill the square, so allow a little time to find a clear view.
text.geographic_location: In Sejongno, Jongno-gu, central Seoul, directly in front of Gyeongbokgung palace. The square runs south from Gwanghwamun Gate, between the Sejong Center for the Performing Arts on the west side and the Kyobo Book Centre on the east.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so head for Gwanghwamun Square in front of Gyeongbokgung. The King Sejong statue stands roughly 250 metres north of the Admiral Yi Sun-sin statue and its fountain. Walk towards Gwanghwamun Gate and you will reach it. Walk to the King Sejong statue, face north and adjust your position on site. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the gate behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the square, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the gate closer behind the king.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the statue, looking north toward Gwanghwamun Gate). The seated King Sejong statue in the foreground, with Gwanghwamun Gate and the trees at the far end of the square behind it. Check the view on your screen on the day and adjust your position slightly if needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the gate sitting above and beyond it. Keep your phone level so the gate does not lean. For a different view, 육조마당 gives pine trees in the foreground with the gate and Bugaksan Mountain behind. Standing at the Admiral Yi Sun-sin statue lets you shoot the whole length of the square, from the fountain up to the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit bronze does not turn bright and flat after dark. Use night mode if your phone offers it, and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the statue is illuminated, is one guide's suggestion. By day the gate and trees show clearly behind the statue.

text.access_note: This is an open public square, but events can close or crowd parts of it, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto zoom (2x-5x) makes distant objects such as the gate look closer to the statue in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop an illuminated statue looking over-bright against a dark sky.
Night mode needs the phone held still for a second or two to give a sharp image.
The square is open to walk through without a ticket, though events may restrict parts of it.

name: N Seoul Tower
label: N Seoul Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Huam-ro (후암로)' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Huam-ro (후암로) nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16474080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Namsan Seoul Tower' (104 m across).
notes: Tower on top of Namsan with views over the city.

text.description:
N Seoul Tower stands on the summit of Namsan in central Seoul. At 236 metres it is a landmark and symbol of the city, and it began as a broadcasting tower. Building started in 1969, and the observation decks were finished in 1975. The public were not let up until October 1980, and the observation levels reopened as N Seoul Tower in December 2005.

Start with the default lens (1x) and keep the tower in the upper part of the picture. If it looks too small, try 2x or 3x. Turn on the gridlines to keep the tower straight. Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky turns pale.

Three other views are worth knowing. On Huam-ro (후암로), on the uphill stretch that leads from Seoul Station exit 11, the tower rises along the slope of the road, which makes a classic Seoul shot. You can also put a person in the frame there: cross the junction in front of the Samsung Dream Scholarship Foundation and have them stand a little way along the pavement. Namsan Park Baekbeom Square gives a wide view of the tower, with a section of the old city wall in the foreground. Dongjak Bridge shows the tower far in the distance, framed by the blue railings, with Subway Line 4 trains crossing the scene.
text.geographic_location: The tower is on the summit of Namsan in central Seoul.
text.directions_text: For the alternative Huam-ro view, leave Seoul Station by exit 11 and walk uphill along Huam-ro. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and its surroundings. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) if you want the tower larger. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if a person stands close to you and you want them big in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Huam-ro (후암로) (uphill stretch leading from Seoul Station exit 11). The tower rising along the slope of the road, a classic street-level Seoul shot that can include you in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the tower in the upper part of the frame. Ask your companion to stand a few steps away, small in the frame. For another angle, try Namsan Park Baekbeom Square, where the old city wall sits in the foreground, or Dongjak Bridge, where the blue railings frame the distant tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Take a few shots, since people and cars move through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good time to try, when the sky is softer. Night mode can help once it is dark, but hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: Huam-ro is an ordinary public street; for going up the tower itself, check the official site before you go, as access and photography rules can change.

name: Bukchon Hanok Village
label: Bukchon Hanok Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '북촌로11길' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of 북촌로11길 nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Bukchon Hanok Village'.
notes: Hillside lanes of traditional Korean houses.

text.description:
Bukchon Hanok Village is a residential neighbourhood of restored traditional Korean houses, called hanok. Many date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Much of what you see today was built around the 1920s, when a Korean developer, Chŏng Segwŏn, put up smaller hanok with modern touches such as glass windows and electricity. Preservation rules from the late 20th century helped save the area as Seoul redeveloped around it.

It photographs well because of the lanes. Curved tile roofs step down the slope in rows, and above them you can see the modern city and Namsan with N Seoul Tower. Another good rooftop view is Gahoe-dong 31, which looks across the hanok roofs to the taller city and palace district beyond.

People still live here. About 6,100 residents share the streets with millions of visitors a year, so keep your voice down, stay out of gateways and do not photograph residents. Some lanes have 'no photo' signs, so obey them. As of January 2025, visitors not staying in local guesthouses can only enter between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.; check current rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: Bukchon Hanok Village is in Jongno District, north of the Cheonggyecheon stream and Jongno. It covers parts of Gahoe-dong, Gye-dong, Jae-dong, Wonseo-dong and Insa-dong.
text.directions_text: The village is served by Anguk station (Line 3). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to squeeze the rooftops and the city behind them together. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole slope in the frame, as it makes the lane look wider and the far buildings smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 북촌로11길 (lower section, shooting up the slope; the upper section is the alternative view looking back south). Curved tile roofs of the hanok rows stepping down the lane, with the modern city and Namsan/N Seoul Tower visible beyond the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the lane's edges as leading lines and let the rooflines fill the upper half of the frame. Turn on gridlines to keep the roofs level. For a different view, try the wide rooftop panorama from Gahoe-dong 31. Keep gateways and residents out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiled roofs to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Stay at 1x or 2x rather than using high digital zoom, which makes tile detail soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, or mid-morning after 10 a.m. If the January 2025 entry hours still apply, visitors not staying locally need to be in before the 5 p.m. cut-off, so check current access rules. The light is softer at these times and tour groups are usually thinner.

text.access_note: This is a residential neighbourhood with public lanes. As of January 2025, visitors not staying in local guesthouses can only enter between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.; check current rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto at 2x or more compresses the view and brings the city behind the rooftops closer.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to exaggerate the width of a narrow lane and make distant buildings look smaller.
Late afternoon and mid-morning light is softer, and tour groups tend to be thinner at those times.
Anguk station (Line 3) is the station named for the village; the walking distance from it is not given.

name: Gwangjang Market
label: Gwangjang Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Starbucks Gwangjang Market' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Gwangjang Market' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/607083156: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gwangjang Market' (292 m across).

text.description: Gwangjang Market is a traditional street market in Jongno District and one of the oldest and largest in South Korea. It began in 1905 as Dongdaemun Market, set up by Korean merchants as the first market to open every day of the week, and it took the name Gwangjang in 1960. Today around 65,000 people pass through on a typical day. It is best known for bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes) and mayak gimbap. For photographs it offers two very different scenes. Inside, the food alley is full of griddles, steam and vendors at work. Outside, the market's Korean-script signage stands above a red-brick wall. Nearby is the third-floor rooftop terrace of Starbucks Gwangjang Market, a restored red-brick warehouse. From there you can stand behind the signage with the sky beyond, away from the crowds in the aisles. Start at the rooftop viewpoint for the wider view, then go down to the arched 광장시장 sign over an entrance, and finish in the food alley. The alley is crowded and lit from overhead, so expect harsh light. Ask vendors' permission before photographing them.
text.geographic_location: Gwangjang Market is in Jongno District, in central Seoul, in the Jongno 5-ga area.
text.directions_text: Reach the market from Jongno 5-ga or Euljiro 4-ga metro station. Ask for the Starbucks at Gwangjang Market; its rooftop is the viewpoint. Gate names vary between guides, so check the gate names on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the signage and brick wall from the rooftop. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the arched entrance sign and the corridor behind it. Use telephoto (2x or more) for close shots of food on the griddles without crowding the vendors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Starbucks Gwangjang Market (rooftop terrace on the third floor, reached by the spiral corridor). From the rooftop you face the market's Korean-script signage rising above the red-brick wall, with the sky behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the signage on one of the lines, leaving plenty of sky above. Keep the red-brick wall along the bottom of the frame. For a second view, go down to the arched 광장시장 sign over the entrance and shoot with the busy corridor opening behind it. In the food alley, aim at the griddles and frying pans, and get the vendors' hands in the shot rather than their faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the signage to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour. In the food alley, tap on the food and use the 1x or 2x view. Try a Live Photo for the sizzling pans.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best for the food alley, which is crowded at midday. The rooftop has a sunset sky view, so late afternoon is worth trying for the signage shot.

text.access_note: The market is a public space, but the rooftop is inside a café, so check the official site before you go to find out whether you can go up without buying anything.
claims_not_in_sources: Food-alley lighting is mostly overhead and can look unflattering.
The market is crowded around midday, and early morning is quieter.
It is polite to ask vendors before photographing them.
The rooftop of the Starbucks building offers a sunset sky view and a quieter break from the food aisles.
Gate names and numbering differ between guides.

name: Lotte World Tower
label: Lotte World Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '석촌호수' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '석촌호수' (relation/9856886): edge nearest the subject (1056 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5162137574: the OpenStreetMap point 'Woori Bank'.

text.description: Lotte World Tower is the tallest building in South Korea: 123 storeys and 555 metres high, and the sixth-tallest in the world. It opened to the public on 3 April 2017. Its pale glass skin is inspired by Korean ceramics and has fine metal accents. Its tapering shape makes it easy to recognise from far away. The best-known view from this spot is across Seokchon Lake, where the tower rises behind the water and, on a calm day, is reflected in the surface. A Seoul guide calls the east side of the lake the best place for an exterior shot, with the reflection at its most striking in late afternoon or at sunset. The lake is also the setting for a cherry blossom festival, held in late March or early April in recent years (5-9 April in 2023, 27-31 March in 2024), and for fireworks shows. Blossom branches in the foreground make a good frame for the tower. The tower is so tall that you will not fit all of it in at close range, so step back along the lake edge and let the water fill the lower part of the picture. Keep your phone upright for the full height, or turn it sideways to take in more of the lake and any trees. The observation decks inside are a separate, ticketed visit. Check the official site before you go if you want to go up.
text.geographic_location: In Sincheon-dong, Songpa District, Seoul, on the shore of Seokchon Lake close to the tower.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground stops listed for this spot, so head for Sincheon-dong in Songpa District by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Seokchon Lake (석촌호수), the east side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the tower, the water and the shoreline together. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the glass top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 석촌호수 (east lake, lake edge facing the tower). The tower rising behind the water, with its reflection on the lake surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower's vertical lines straight. Place the water's edge on the lower third line so the reflection has room. In blossom season, use a branch at the edge of the frame. The lake has other good spots close by: the tower lit up at night across the water, and the tower framed by cherry trees in bloom. Both are worth a short walk if you have time.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Wait for ripples to settle before taking the shot. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a rail to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when the reflection is at its best. After dark, the lit tower seen across the lake is also worth a try.

text.access_note: The lake edge is an open public park; the observation decks (Seoul Sky) in the tower are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The tower's tapering shape makes it easy to recognise from far away.
You cannot fit the whole tower in the frame at close range.
The reflection is clearest when the water is calm.
Cherry blossom branches in the foreground make a good frame for the tower.
The stand-here point is about 130 m, a couple of minutes on foot, from the mapped subject point (133 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
The lake edge is an open public area that can be walked along without a ticket.
Crowds tend to be heavy at weekends and during the April blossom.

name: Cheonggyecheon
label: Cheonggyecheon
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10718843: large area 'Cheonggyecheon Stream' (4188 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Cheonggyecheon is a 10.9-kilometre stream running through the middle of downtown Seoul, with paths and public space alongside it. It has an unusual story. In the late 1950s the stream was covered with concrete, and an elevated expressway was later built on top of it, opened in stages between 1969 and 1976. In 2003 the city began removing the road and bringing the stream back, and it reopened to the public in September 2005. That history is part of what makes it photograph well: you are standing in a sunken ribbon of water and greenery with the city rising on both sides. The water is shallow and calm, and the banks have stepping stones, bridges and planting, so there is always something to put in the foreground. Keep the stream as the leading line in your picture and let the bridges or the buildings above frame it. For people shots, wait a moment for a gap in the walkers, because this is a popular route with residents and visitors. Take care near the water's edge and on any stepping stones, and keep a hand on your phone when you lean over a railing.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Seoul, where the stream runs west to east through the city centre.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Seoul and walk to the stream. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the stream and its banks as you see them. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole channel, the bridges and the buildings above in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a bridge or a stretch of water further along.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cheonggye Plaza (western starting point, by the Spring sculpture). The red-and-blue Spring sculpture in the foreground with the two-tier waterfall running down into the stream. The stream runs west to east, so looking west is looking upstream. Keep to the paths and avoid blocking other walkers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water along a diagonal or on the lower third line so it leads the eye into the picture. Crouch slightly to bring the surface of the water and any stepping stones into the foreground. Try one frame with a bridge arching across the top, then one tighter shot with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the brightest part of the scene to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the sky down slightly so the banks keep their detail. If you take a Live Photo, hold still for a couple of seconds and you may catch moving water. Portrait mode works well for a person with the stream behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the paths are quieter, such as early in the morning, for clear frames of the water. Come back in the evening for a different mood, and use night mode if the light is low, keeping the phone steady against a railing.

text.access_note: This is a stream and public space in downtown Seoul, but check the official site before you go in case of closures, events or high water.

name: Insa-dong
label: Insa-dong
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/415153837: the OpenStreetMap point 'Insa-dong'.
notes: Street of traditional shops, teahouses and galleries.

text.description: Insa-dong is a neighbourhood in Seoul's Jongno District, and its main street is Insadong-gil. Narrow alleys lead off the street to galleries and tea shops, and many of the older buildings that were once homes for merchants and officials are now restaurants and shops. That mix of traditional roofs, hand-painted signs and busy shopfronts gives you plenty to frame on a phone. The area covers about 12.7 hectares, so you can wander it on foot without planning much. It began roughly 500 years ago as a residential area for government officials. It later became Korea's largest market for antiques and artwork, and it still holds many of the country's antique shops, galleries and traditional stationery shops. Ssamziegil, a handcrafts shopping centre that opened in 2004, is a well-known stop, and the street-food stalls make good close-up subjects. Look for the unusual Starbucks with its sign written in Korean, a small example of how the neighbourhood adapts modern names to its own style. For photographs, work with layers: a shopfront sign in the foreground, the crowd in the middle and rooftops behind. Step into a side alley for quieter pictures with fewer people in the frame. Keep your phone ready for small details too, such as lanterns, tea-house doorways and craft displays. Public streets are fine for photographs, but ask before photographing people up close or inside shops.
text.geographic_location: Insa-dong is in Jongno District, Seoul. It is bordered by Gwanhun-dong to the north, Nagwon-dong to the east and Gongpyeong-dong to the west, with Jongno 2-ga and Jeokseon-dong to the south.
text.directions_text: Jonggak, Jongno 3-ga and Anguk stations serve the area. Head for Insa-dong in Jongno District and make for the main street, Insadong-gil. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes, because it keeps shopfronts and signs looking natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrower alleys, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for lanterns, signs and rooftop details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take a few frames from here, then walk towards it and keep shooting along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the street's vertical lines, such as sign posts and building edges, straight. Put a shop sign or lantern in the foreground and let the street fade behind it. Use telephoto for compressed, close crops of crafts and food stalls. In the busiest stretches, wait a moment for gaps in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a sign or a shopfront to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright signs or the sky wash out. Use portrait mode only with people's permission, and Live Photos for moving crowds or street performers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early on a weekday morning is likely to be calmer. In the evening, lit signs and shop windows can look good, so switch on night mode if your phone offers it.

text.access_note: Insadong-gil is a public street lined with shops, galleries and restaurants; for any individual building or gallery, check the official site before you go.

name: Changdeokgung Palace
label: Changdeokgung
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/789965985: large area 'Changdeokgung Palace' (1277 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: UNESCO-listed palace with the Secret Garden.

text.description:
Changdeokgung is a former royal palace in Seoul and one of the best preserved of all Korean palaces. It was founded in 1405 as the second palace in the city, after Gyeongbokgung, and its name means "Palace of Prospering Virtue". Many Joseon kings preferred to live here rather than in the official main palace. After all the city's palaces burned down in 1592, Changdeokgung was rebuilt and served as the main palace for several centuries. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

It photographs well because it is a spread of low, tiled halls, gateways and courtyards rather than one big building, so you can make many different pictures: a pitched roof against the sky, a carved gate, a long view across a stone-paved yard. The subject is the palace as a whole, and the grounds are large, so treat the phone icon on the map as your starting spot and then wander.

For phone photos, look for lines and repeating shapes, such as rows of roof tiles, painted eaves and doorways that frame the buildings beyond. Keep people out of the edges of the frame where you can, and take a few wide shots and a few close ones of the colourful beam work. The Secret Garden is part of the palace, but some sections need a booked tour, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Changdeokgung is in central Seoul, east of Gyeongbokgung palace, and it sits right next to its neighbour Changgyeonggung. Together the two are known as the "East Palace".
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the phone icon on the map. From there, the palace is 78 m to the east, about 1 minute on foot. Check the official site for the entrance to use. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in courtyards and by gateways, where you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, painted eaves and other details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the horizontal rooflines with them, keeping the camera level so the buildings do not lean. Use a gateway or a doorway as a natural frame for the halls behind it. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a closer one of a single roof or decorated beam.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the roof tiles and painted wood do not wash out. Portrait mode is better kept for people than for the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the roofs and fewer harsh shadows in the courtyards. Go as early as the palace allows if you want fewer people in your frame.

text.access_note: This is a UNESCO-listed palace and some sections, such as parts of the Secret Garden, need a booked tour, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dongdaemun Design Plaza
label: Dongdaemun Design Plaz
camera_source: Commons cluster (2 photos), weak. Moved 48 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10647068: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dongdaemun Design Plaza' (332 m across).

text.description:
Dongdaemun Design Plaza, usually called DDP, is a huge, smooth, silvery building that looks more like a landscape than a block. It was designed by Zaha Hadid and opened on 21 March 2014. Its curving, flowing surfaces give a phone plenty to work with: long sweeping lines, soft reflections and almost no straight edges. The main building is 280 metres long, with three underground levels and four above ground, so one frame will never hold all of it. The best photos come from choosing a piece of it and letting the curves lead the eye.

The site has a lot of history behind it. Dongdaemun Stadium stood here from 1925 until 2007, and parts of the old Seoul fortress wall have been restored nearby. Dongdaemun History & Culture Park lies on the east side of the building, which gives you older stonework to set against the modern shapes. The roof is a walkable park, so you can also look at the building from above as well as from the ground.

For photos, step back as far as the space allows and use the ultra-wide lens for the big sweep. Then move closer and look for repeating panels, curved edges and people walking through the frame for scale. Keep the phone level, since tilting it will bend the long lines.
text.geographic_location: Dongdaemun Design Plaza is in the Dongdaemun area of central Seoul, which is known for its fashion district. It stands on the former Dongdaemun Stadium site, next to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park.
text.directions_text: The building is physically connected to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station on Seoul Subway Lines 2, 4 and 5, so that is the simplest way to arrive. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the building. Use the default lens (1x) for sections of the curves, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as panel patterns and edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Miraero Bridge. The curved silver facade of DDP framed by the walkway, making the building look large and light at the same time. Turn to face west and walk a few steps back if you want more of it in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line a curved edge up with a grid line or diagonal. Keep the phone level so the long lines do not lean. Include a person or two for scale. For a different view, walk to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park on the east side and set the old stone against the modern shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the silver surfaces keep their detail. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is calmer, with fewer people in the frame. Around dusk and after dark the building's curves can look striking with the lights on.

text.access_note: The outside areas and park are generally open to walk around, but exhibitions and some indoor areas may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is likely to be quieter than the middle of the day.
The building is likely to look good around dusk and after dark with its lighting on.
Tilting the phone will make the building's long lines appear to lean.

name: Jogyesa Temple
label: Jogyesa Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '대웅전' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '대웅전' (way/432721256): middle (49 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223157537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jogyesa Temple' (223 m across).
notes: Main temple of Korean Seon Buddhism, hung with lanterns.

text.description: Jogyesa is the chief temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, set in the middle of downtown Seoul. A temple was first founded here in 1395, and it became the order's chief temple in 1936. The photo that works best is the front of the Main Buddha Hall, the Daeungjeon, seen from the entrance courtyard. Its gables and eaves are painted in dancheong, the traditional bright patterns, and the courtyard around it is hung with lanterns. If the doors are open, you can see the golden Buddha from outside. The hall was built in 1938 from pine wood from Baekdu Mountain. Two trees about 500 years old stand in the courtyard, a white pine and a Chinese scholar tree, and either one makes a good foreground. The lantern displays are seasonal. Lotus lanterns go up in the weeks before Buddha's Birthday, usually in May, and in the evening they make the courtyard glow. At other times of year you will see far fewer lanterns, so judge the date before you plan the shot. This is a working temple, so keep to the outdoor areas, stay outside during services and avoid photographing monks. For a second angle, the bell pavilion (Beomjongnu) gives a higher, wider view over the courtyard.
text.geographic_location: Jogyesa is in Gyeonji-dong, in Seoul's Jongno District. It is in the Insa-dong area, near Gyeongbokgung Palace.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so use a map app on your phone to reach Jogyesa Temple in Gyeonji-dong, in the Insa-dong area of Jongno District. Enter through the Iljumun, the one-pillar gate, and walk into the main courtyard. The Main Buddha Hall is found by walking the courtyard, so allow a little time to move around and find your angle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the hall, the lanterns and the courtyard into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the hall front. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the painted eaves and woodwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the entrance courtyard, facing the front of the hall). The main hall's dancheong-painted gables and eaves, framed by the lantern-hung courtyard, with the golden Buddha visible through the open doors if you shoot from outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the roofline level, so the hall does not lean. Use hanging lanterns or a branch of one of the old trees as a frame at the top of the picture. For a different view, go to the bell pavilion (Beomjongnu). From its steps you look across the courtyard, with Geungnakjeon on the left and the Daeungjeon in the centre. The gate was reported closed on at least one visit, so the top of the steps may be as far as you can go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the painted colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode for the lanterns. Brace your elbows against your body and keep still while it captures. Avoid flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Lanterns hang in the weeks before Buddha's Birthday, usually in May, and they are lit in the evening, so that is the time for glowing shots. Outside that season, visit in daylight for the colours of the woodwork.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so stay outside the hall during services and avoid photographing monks. Check the official site before you go for current access and photography rules.

name: Gwanghwamun Gate
label: Gwanghwamun Gate
camera_source: Commons cluster (46 photos). Moved 85 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 130 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/170199440: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gwanghwamun Gate' (34 m across).
notes: The main south gate of Gyeongbokgung.

text.description:
Gwanghwamun is the main, south-facing gate of Gyeongbokgung palace, and it is the easiest way to get a classic Seoul photo without going inside anything. The gate is about 34 m across, with a painted, tiled roof above heavy stone. It stands at the top of the wide, open Gwanghwamun Plaza, so you can step back far enough to fit it in. The long approach also gives your picture a clear centre line, and the gate sits neatly in the middle of it.

The gate was first completed in 1395 and was named by Sejong the Great in 1426. It was destroyed in 1592 and burned again during the Korean War. The version you see now was rebuilt in wood and put back on its original alignment, with the restoration opening to the public on 15 August 2010. The nameplate was reworked in 2023 as gold characters on a black field. Look for the stone haetae statue in front of the gate, a legendary animal said to guard against fire and evil spirits. It makes a good foreground detail.

A ceremonial changing of the guard is held in front of the gate, which adds colour if you are there for it. Check the official site before you go for current times. Keep people in the frame for scale, but expect crowds in the middle of the day.
text.geographic_location: Gwanghwamun is in Jongno District, central Seoul, at the northern end of Sejongno and Gwanghwamun Plaza. It is the south entrance to Gyeongbokgung palace.
text.directions_text: Head for Gwanghwamun Plaza, at the southern approach to the gate. The nearest Seoul Subway stop to the gate is Gyeongbokgung Station on Line 3. Gwanghwamun Station on Line 5 is at the southern end of the plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and plaza together. Then try telephoto (2x-3x) to fill the frame with the gate. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk much closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gwanghwamun Square (광화문광장) (north end, standing in front of the King Sejong statue and facing the gate). The gate in the middle distance, with Bugaksan Mountain rising behind it and the bronze statue beside the frame. You will see the whole front of the gate with the open plaza in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the central gate opening on the middle line so the picture looks balanced. At 1x the gate will look small, so try 2x-3x to bring it closer. For a second picture, walk closer and crouch slightly with the haetae statue in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the roofline stays straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the roof tiles and painted details keep their colour. Take a few frames when people walk through, then keep the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people. Because the gate faces south, the front tends to be well lit from late morning into the afternoon. In the evening, try night mode if the gate is lit.

text.access_note: The plaza in front of the gate is a public open space, but check the official site before you go for palace entry rules and guard ceremony times.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually less crowded at the gate.
Because the gate faces south, its front tends to be well lit from late morning into the afternoon.
The gate may be lit in the evening.
From about 133 m away at 1x the gate appears fairly small in the frame, so 2x-3x helps.
The haetae statue works as a foreground detail.

name: Deoksugung Palace
label: Deoksugung
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '덕수궁 돌담길' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '중화전' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26658458: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Deoksugung Palace' (429 m across).
notes: Palace next to Seoul City Hall mixing Korean and Western architecture.

text.description:
Deoksugung was the main palace of the Korean Empire (1897–1910), and it mixes traditional Korean halls with Western-style buildings. Emperor Gojong expanded it quickly in those years, and the throne hall Junghwajeon and the Western-style Seokjojeon both date from his time. It began life as a temporary royal home during the 1592–1598 Imjin War and was renamed Deoksugung in 1907. One scholar estimates it is now only about a third of its peak size, which is why the palace feels tucked into the modern city around it.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is from outside the gates. The long granite wall runs along the pavement with street trees arching overhead, and the lines lead the eye down the path. Tall modern buildings show toward Jeongdong-gil, so the old and new city sit in one frame. Stand on the opposite side of the walkway from the wall so the wall and the trees fit together. The road beside it is narrow and has traffic, so stay on the pavement and never step into the road to get the shot.

If you go inside, Seokjojeon's Western-style front looks good framed by the fountain, and Junghwajeon's roofline and stairs work well from the courtyard with the traditional gate behind you. Entry to the grounds may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Deoksugung sits in the middle of Seoul, in the busy city centre beside the Jeongdong-gil area. The famous stone-wall road is a separate viewpoint along the palace's outer edge, on the pavement outside the grounds.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Jeongdong-gil area in central Seoul, by taxi or on foot. Look for the long granite wall with street trees along it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the wall, trees and path look natural. If the pavement feels tight, try ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the wall away from the edges of the frame. Telephoto (2x or more) can pack the receding wall and trees closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 덕수궁 돌담길 (wall-side pavement, shooting from the opposite side of the walkway). The palace's long granite wall with street trees overhead, receding down the path, with modern Seoul buildings visible toward Jeongdong-gil. Stay on the pavement, as the road is narrow and has traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the wall running diagonally through the frame so it recedes down the path, and let the tree branches form a canopy at the top. Turn gridlines on to keep the wall's top edge level. If you also go inside the grounds, Seokjojeon's Western-style front framed by the fountain and Junghwajeon's roofline from the courtyard make good alternative shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky or patches of sun wash out the leaves. Hold the phone steady and take a few frames, as passers-by will move through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk gives low side light on the wall, and overcast days give even tones. Early morning or a rainy day is usually quieter.

text.access_note: The wall-side pavement is an ordinary public street, but the palace grounds (including Seokjojeon and Junghwajeon) are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Jongmyo Shrine
label: Jongmyo Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '월대' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '월대' (node/11265948889): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19286505: large area 'Jongmyo Shrine' (768 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Confucian shrine to the Joseon kings, UNESCO World Heritage.

text.description: Jongmyo is the royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon dynasty, where memorial services were held for deceased kings and queens. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1995. Its main hall, Jeongjeon, is the longest building of traditional design in Korea, and the shrine's plain, repeating shapes suit a phone camera well. The most memorable view is from the edge of the stone terrace, the 월대 (Woldae), in front of Jeongjeon. From there you see the long row of dark columns and the unbroken roofline, with the open stone platform in the foreground. That wide foreground helps show how long the building is. The courtyard in front of the hall measures 150 metres by 100 metres, so there is room to step back and take your time. The buildings were rebuilt in 1601 after the older shrine burned down in the Japanese invasions of the 1590s. If you have a few minutes to spare, two other spots are worth a look. The Mangmyoru pavilion gives a wider view across the courtyards and rooflines, with a pond and greenery in front. The lane called Seosunra-gil runs along the shrine's old stone wall, framed by trees and sometimes seasonal leaves. Photography is not allowed inside Jeongjeon or Yeongnyeongjeon, and rules elsewhere in the grounds may vary, so follow the signs. Keep off any stones marked as the spirit path.
text.geographic_location: Jongmyo stands in the Jongno District of central Seoul, just south of the palaces of Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung. Since 2019 a road tunnel has let visitors walk between the shrine and the palaces.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Jongno District in central Seoul and ask for Jongmyo Shrine. A taxi is a simple option, and it helps to have the name in Korean (종묘) ready to show the driver. Inside the paid grounds, the 월대, the stone terrace in front of the main hall, Jeongjeon, is the viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole length of Jeongjeon in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view of part of the hall. Telephoto (2x-5x) works for details such as the columns and roof tiles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 월대 (edge of the stone terrace in front of Jeongjeon, facing the hall). Jeongjeon's long row of dark columns and unbroken roofline, framed by the open stone platform in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the roofline level with a horizontal line so the building does not tilt. Include some of the stone platform at the bottom of the frame, since it shows how long the hall is. For a different view, Mangmyoru gives a wide shot across the courtyards and rooflines with the pond in front. The lane called Seosunra-gil runs along the shrine's old stone wall, framed by trees and sometimes seasonal leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: The hall's columns are dark, so tap on the building to focus and then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky turns white. Do not use the phone inside Jeongjeon or Yeongnyeongjeon, where photography is prohibited.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the dark columns and the roofline. Visits to the main halls are usually by guided tour, so your time at the terrace may be set by the tour. Check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed World Heritage site where the main halls are usually reached on guided tours, and one guide says it closes on Tuesdays, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide (0.5x) lens is likely needed to fit the whole length of Jeongjeon from the terrace edge.
Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer and kinder to the dark columns.
Dark columns can make a phone darken the building or blow out the sky, so lowering exposure may help.
A taxi driver will understand the Korean name 종묘.

name: Myeongdong Cathedral
label: Myeongdong Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Myeongdong Shopping Street' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Myeongdong Shopping Street' (node/12894590901): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/355630939: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Myeongdong Cathedral' (384 m across).

text.description: Myeongdong Cathedral is the national cathedral of the Archdiocese of Seoul and the seat of its archbishop. It was dedicated on 29 May 1898, and when it was built it was the largest building in Seoul. The government listed it as Historic Site No. 258 in November 1977. Today it sits in the middle of one of the busiest shopping districts in the city, and that contrast is what makes this spot work. The quiet old building and the bright, busy street fit into one frame, and the picture tells you something about the neighbourhood. After dark the cathedral is lit, and the street lights and signs add colour around it. Around Christmas there are also LED rose displays. Expect crowds at peak times and at Christmas, so allow a little patience for a clear view. If you would rather have a classic shot, try the front stairs, where the bell tower and spire can be framed against the sky. There is also a calmer garden spot where the street noise fades behind the spire.
text.geographic_location: Myeongdong Cathedral is in the Myeongdong neighbourhood of Jung District, in central Seoul.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for the Myeongdong neighbourhood in Jung District and use a map app. The cathedral lies to the east, about 220 m away, a short walk from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the street and the cathedral together. Try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the cathedral closer between the buildings. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of the street in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Myeongdong Shopping Street. The cathedral with the busy shopping-street buildings as a side frame or backdrop, a contrast of old and new. The photo shows the old church against the modern district around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the shopfronts on one or both sides as a frame and keep the cathedral's spire near the centre or on a gridline. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you can. For a different view, the front stairs give a shot of the red-brick facade and bell tower with the spire against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings straight. Tap the cathedral to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lit church does not wash out against the dark sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady, leaning on a wall or post if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the cathedral is lit and the street lights add colour. Around Christmas it is especially popular, so expect more people.

text.access_note: The outside of the cathedral is open to the public all day, but photography inside is not allowed during services, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go in.

name: Seoullo 7017
label: Seoullo 7017
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '서울역 광장' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '서울역5번출구' (pois).
notes: Former overpass turned into an elevated garden walkway.

text.description:
Seoullo 7017 is a raised walkway in the middle of Seoul, built on top of an old highway overpass that closed in 2015. It is about 1 kilometre long, sits some 17 metres above the street, and is planted with around 24,000 plants. The Dutch firm MVRDV designed it, and it opened in May 2017. The name comes from 1970, the year the overpass was dedicated, and 2017, the year the walkway opened. The 17 also refers to the number of walkways connected to it.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is not on the walkway at all. It is from the square in front of the old Seoul Station building, 서울역 광장. From there you see the old station in the foreground, with the bustle of the station behind it, and the walkway about 140 metres to the east. It is the view tourism guides recommend for a souvenir shot. The walkway itself is not the main subject here, so treat it as a green line across the city scene.

If you want the plants and the city lights, walk up and try the rose garden area (장미광장). It gives raised views over the surrounding downtown, with flowers close to the lens as a foreground. Wherever you stand, look for a clear foreground, keep the phone level, and take a few frames so you can pick the best one later.
text.geographic_location: Seoullo 7017 is in central Seoul, cutting diagonally across the area around Seoul Station. It runs from Malli-dong in the south-west towards Namdaemun and Hoehyeon Station in the north-east.
text.directions_text: Start from Seoul Station, the well-known landmark here, and go to the square in front of the old station building. From the square, the walkway is about 2 minutes on foot to the east. The nearest stairway up is across the street from the front of the station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the old station and the walkway together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building will not fit, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the walkway and its plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 서울역 광장 (in front of the old Seoul Station building). The old Seoul Station building in the foreground with the station's bustle behind it; the walkway itself is not the main subject. From the square you see the old station with the station bustle behind it, rather than the walkway from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the old station building on one third of the frame, with the raised walkway and sky filling the rest. Hold the phone level so the building edges stay straight. For a different view, the rose garden area (장미광장) on the walkway gives elevated views over downtown with plants in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the old station building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky turns white. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone against something steady, or lean on a railing, for sharper lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime suits the old station building. Around dusk and into the evening, the lit walkway and the lights of the station and downtown make a more colourful picture.

text.access_note: The square is open public space and the walkway is a public park, but opening times and any closures can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Daytime light suits the old station building, while dusk and evening show the lit walkway and city lights at their best.
Night mode works better if the phone is rested against something steady, such as a railing.

name: Bosingak
label: Bosingak Belfry
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '보신각' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '보신각' (way/141957163): middle (93 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q487603: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pavilion housing the bell of Jongno.

text.description: Bosingak is a two-storey red-and-green bell pavilion standing on Jongno, a busy street in the middle of Seoul. It photographs well because of the contrast. The traditional painted roofs sit in the foreground, and modern office towers rise straight behind them, so one frame shows old and new Seoul together. Its bell gave Jongno its name, which means 'bell street'. The pavilion was first built in 1395 and has been destroyed several times by war and fire. In the Joseon period the bell was struck to mark the opening and closing of the city gates. Today it is famously rung at midnight on New Year's Eve, when very large crowds gather. The bell that hangs in the pavilion now is a replica. The original, cast in 1468, is kept in the National Museum of Korea. Start with the default lens (1x) and keep the whole building in view with the towers behind it. Then try stepping back for a wider view with trees around the roof. Traffic and pedestrians pass all day, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. The bell itself can be hard to see from outside the pavilion, so treat the building as your subject.
text.geographic_location: Bosingak is on Jongno in central Seoul, at the Jongno crossroads, with office towers close behind it.
text.directions_text: Bosingak stands on Jongno in central Seoul. Ask for Bosingak (보신각) on Jongno. On New Year's Eve, Line 1 trains do not stop at Jonggak Station because of the crowds, so plan another way to arrive. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pavilion with the towers behind. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds force you to stand close. Try telephoto (2x or more) from further back to pick out the roof against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the pavilion, at the Jongno crossroads). The two-storey red-and-green pavilion in the foreground, with modern office towers rising behind it for a traditional-versus-modern contrast.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the pavilion's roofline level. Place the building in the lower half of the frame so the towers show above it and the old-versus-new contrast reads clearly. For a softer alternative, step back and take the pavilion from a distance with the green trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the roof colours. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the pavilion is lit, makes for an atmospheric shot. Daytime also works well for the colours. New Year's Eve around midnight is the famous moment, but it is very crowded.

text.access_note: The pavilion is on a public street and is easily viewed from outside, but check the official site before you go for any access rules, especially around New Year's Eve.
claims_not_in_sources: The pavilion is illuminated in the evening (one guide says so).
Green trees around the pavilion are visible from a distance.
Modern office towers stand directly behind the pavilion from the stand-here point.
The bell is hard to see from outside the pavilion (one guide says so).
The pavilion can be viewed from the street without entering.
Traffic and pedestrians pass all day at the crossroads.
